Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

vignette:
Amina was 20 years old, African-American, and working as a pharmacist when she first came for help, though she spoke about herself as if she were still living in the weeks after the event that had changed her sense of safety. She had been taken by armed men and held in captivity, where she was repeatedly forced to do things against her will and humiliated through punishment and control. What she remembered most clearly was not a full, ordered story but fragments: a harsh command, the sting of fear in her body, and the fixed sense of being trapped in a position she could not get out of. When she tried to describe it, she stopped often and said there were pieces missing, as if she could reach the edge of the memory but not the whole shape of it. The parts that did return did not feel like distant recollection. They arrived bodily. At times, when a thought or image came unbidden, she felt as though her body was back in that same position again, tense and constrained, with the same helpless dread pressing through her chest and limbs. She would begin to explain and then trail off, saying she could not put it into words because language seemed too small for what had happened.

In the months afterward, Amina found herself reacting strongly to certain moments that other people took for granted. Water was one of the clearest. Seeing flooding on the news, standing near a large body of water, or even passing a place where water gathered after rain could make her feel suddenly uneasy and pulled into the memory of being overpowered and unable to move freely. Arguments were another potent trigger. Raised voices, sharp disagreement, or the feeling that someone was pressing her into an unwanted decision could send her into a state of immediate alarm, with her attention narrowing to escape and protection. She had also become highly distressed by any experience of being forced to do something, even when the demand was ordinary. She described a deep, immediate resistance in her body whenever she felt pushed, as though compliance meant surrendering safety.

Amina’s days had gradually become organized around staying ahead of danger. She always looked for exits before she could relax in any room, including at work, where she would note the nearest door in the pharmacy, the path to the back corridor, and whether she could leave quickly if needed. She was constantly scanning her surroundings for signs that something was wrong, watching faces, gestures, and the movements of strangers more closely than before. At night, this same vigilance made it difficult to fall asleep. She said she needed to stay alert, and even when she was exhausted she would lie awake listening, checking, and waiting. Her sleep became more complicated because she also began to avoid the parts of the day and the situations that seemed to bring on nightmares. If a late evening conversation turned heavy, or if she knew she was heading into a stretch of tiredness that had previously ended in disturbing dreams, she would try to distract herself or delay sleep as long as possible.

She also found herself avoiding people who had been involved in the event or anyone who looked similar to them. In public, she would sometimes cross the aisle in a store or lower her head if someone’s face, posture, or voice reminded her of them. This had made ordinary life smaller and more effortful, and her relationship had been affected by how quickly she became tense when she felt cornered or argued with. She was aware that the change was visible to others, but she also carried a harsh private judgment about herself. She told herself that she deserved to suffer because of what happened, and that belief made it harder for her to accept comfort or imagine that relief was something she was allowed to seek. She was also haunted by guilt that she had survived when others had not, a thought that returned most sharply in quiet moments and made her feel as if her own continued life was somehow an offense.

By the time she came to treatment, Amina said she was tired of living in a state of constant watchfulness. She came because she was struggling to sleep, because she felt on guard all the time, and because the nights had become especially difficult when nightmares seemed to wait for the same vulnerable hours she was already trying to avoid. She wanted to feel less trapped by the memory and less terrified by ordinary things like water, arguments, and being told what to do. More than anything, she said she hoped not to spend the rest of her life braced for harm, while fearing that if she let herself think about what happened, she would not be able to handle it.
